requirements: The core contributions of 'SmoothQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Large Language Models' have been reproduced, including the SmoothQuant migration transformation, the O1-O3 quantization settings, the INT8 W8A8 quantization flow for transformer blocks, and the accuracy, speedup, and memory experiments across OPT, BLOOM, GLM-130B, MT-NLG 530B, and additional LLM families.

sub_tasks.requirements: The SmoothQuant algorithm has been correctly implemented, including the per-channel smoothing factor with migration strength alpha, the mathematically equivalent scale migration from activations to weights, offline calibration, and fusion into preceding layers.

The mathematically equivalent transformation Y = (X diag(s)^-1) · (diag(s) W) = X̂Ŵ (Equation 3) has been implemented, where a per-channel smoothing factor vector s in R^{C_i} divides the input activation channel-wise and multiplies the corresponding weight input-channel dimension, preserving the exact output Y of the original linear layer.

The per-channel smoothing factor formula s_j = max(|X_j|)^alpha / max(|W_j|)^(1-alpha) (Equation 4) has been implemented, where j indexes input channels, X_j is the activation channel's calibration statistics, and W_j is the corresponding weight channel's statistics.

The migration strength hyperparameter alpha is configurable and correctly controls the balance of quantization difficulty migrated from activations to weights, with alpha closer to 1 pushing more difficulty to weights and alpha closer to 0 pushing more difficulty to activations, as described in Section 4.
The default migration strength alpha = 0.5 is used for all OPT and BLOOM models as the well-balanced point for evenly splitting quantization difficulty, as stated in Section 4.
A larger migration strength alpha = 0.75 is used specifically for GLM-130B because its activations have more significant outliers (~30% outlier channels), as stated in Section 4 and Section 5.1.
A suitable alpha is obtained by running a grid search on a subset of the Pile validation set, as described in Section 5.1 (Activation smoothing).

The smoothing factors and static quantization step sizes are calibrated once offline using 512 random sentences from the Pile pre-training dataset, and the same smoothed and quantized model is then applied for all downstream zero-shot evaluation tasks, as described in Section 5.1.

The per-channel division by diag(s) applied to the input activation X is fused into the parameters of the preceding layer (e.g., linear layer or LayerNorm) offline, so that no additional runtime scaling kernel call overhead is incurred, as described in Section 4.

For cases where the input to a smoothed linear layer originates from a residual add rather than a preceding linear/LayerNorm layer, an extra scaling operation is added to the residual branch (similar to Wei et al. 2022's Outlier Suppression), as described in Section 4.

The implementation reproduces the two extreme failure modes described in Section 4: setting s_j = max(|X_j|) (pushing all difficulty to weights) or s_j = 1/max(|W_j|) (pushing all difficulty to activations) both lead to large accuracy degradation, motivating the need for the balanced alpha formulation, consistent with Figure 10's ablation.

The extreme case s_j = max(|X_j|) (equivalent to alpha=1 in Equation 4, pushing all quantization difficulty from activations to weights) has been implemented and evaluated, and it is confirmed to produce large accuracy degradation because the outlier channels are fully migrated into the weights, making weight quantization difficult, as described in Section 4.

The extreme case s_j = 1/max(|W_j|) (equivalent to alpha=0 in Equation 4, pushing all quantization difficulty from weights to activations) has been implemented and evaluated, and it is confirmed to produce large accuracy degradation because the activation quantization errors dominate, as described in Section 4.

The migration strength alpha sweep ablation has been executed on OPT-175B evaluated with LAMBADA, covering a range of alpha values including the extremes (alpha close to 0 and alpha close to 1) and intermediate values, reproducing the experimental setup underlying Figure 10.

Figure 10 has been reproduced showing that when alpha is too small (<0.4) activations are hard to quantize and accuracy degrades, when alpha is too large (>0.6) weights are hard to quantize and accuracy degrades, and only within the sweet-spot region of alpha between 0.4 and 0.6 both weights and activations achieve small quantization errors and model performance is maintained close to FP16, consistent with Section 4 and Figure 10's ablation on OPT-175B with LAMBADA.

Figure 10 shows that when migration strength alpha is too small (<0.4) on OPT-175B with LAMBADA, the activations become hard to quantize, leading to model accuracy degradation, consistent with Section 5.5 ablation study.

Figure 10 shows that when migration strength alpha is too large (>0.6) on OPT-175B with LAMBADA, the weights become hard to quantize, leading to model accuracy degradation, consistent with Section 5.5 ablation study.

Figure 10 shows that only within the sweet-spot region of alpha between 0.4 and 0.6 on OPT-175B with LAMBADA, both weights and activations achieve small quantization errors and model performance is maintained close to FP16, consistent with Section 5.5 ablation study.

The INT8 W8A8 quantization flow for transformer blocks and the O1-O3 quantization settings (plus baseline schemes) have been implemented, including INT8 linear and BMM operators with CUTLASS INT8 GEMM kernels and FP16 for lightweight ops.

The basic INT8 uniform quantization formula (Equation 1) has been implemented: X_bar^INT8 = round(X^FP16 / Delta) where Delta = max(|X|) / (2^(N-1) - 1), with N=8, correctly handling the symmetric-at-zero assumption for simplicity, as specified in Section 2.

The rounding function (denoted by the ceiling-with-brackets notation in Equation 1) is implemented as round-to-nearest-integer applied to X^FP16 / Delta, producing the quantized integer values, as specified in Section 2 Equation 1.
The quantization step size Delta is computed as max(|X|) / (2^(N-1) - 1), using the maximum absolute value of the tensor X, as specified in Equation 1 of Section 2.

The number of bits N is set to 8 (INT8 quantization) in the quantization formula Delta = max(|X|) / (2^(N-1) - 1), consistent with the paper's focus on INT8 uniform quantization as stated in Section 2.

The quantizer implementation assumes the tensor is symmetric at 0 for simplicity (no zero-point offset), as explicitly stated in Section 2: 'Here we assume the tensor is symmetric at 0 for simplicity; the discussion is similar for asymmetric cases (e.g., after ReLU) by adding a zero-point.'

The activation smoothing computation via migration strength alpha has been implemented to compute the per-channel smoothing factor s_j = max(|X_j|)^alpha / max(|W_j|)^(1-alpha), exactly as given in Equation 4 of Section 4, using the per-channel calibration statistics max(|X_j|) for activations and max(|W_j|) for weights.

Both static quantization (Delta computed offline using calibration samples from the pre-training dataset) and dynamic quantization (Delta computed at runtime from activation statistics) have been implemented, as described in Section 2.

The three quantization granularity levels described in Section 2 and Figure 3 — per-tensor (single step size for the entire matrix), per-token (different step size per token/row of activations), and per-channel (different step size per output channel of weights) — have been implemented as configurable quantization modes.

The per-tensor quantization granularity mode has been implemented, using a single quantization step size Delta for the entire activation or weight matrix, as described in Section 2 and illustrated in Figure 3.

The per-token quantization granularity mode has been implemented, using a different quantization step size for the activations associated with each token (i.e., each row of the T x Ci activation matrix X), as described in Section 2 and illustrated in Figure 3.

The per-channel quantization granularity mode has been implemented, using a different quantization step size for each output channel of the weight matrix W (i.e., each column of the Ci x Co weight matrix), as described in Section 2 and illustrated in Figure 3.

The group-wise quantization mode has been implemented as a coarser-grained version of per-channel quantization, using different quantization step sizes for different channel groups (rather than one step size per individual channel), as described in Section 2 (citing Shen et al., 2020; Yao et al., 2022) and used by the ZeroQuant baseline configuration.

The quantization implementation exposes the granularity level (per-tensor, per-token, per-channel, or group-wise) as a configurable option/parameter that can be independently selected for weights and activations, enabling the construction of the different baseline and SmoothQuant quantization schemes shown in Table 2 (e.g., per-tensor weight + per-token dynamic activation for SmoothQuant-O1).

The post-GEMM rescaling formulation (Equation 2) has been implemented: Y = diag(Delta_X^FP16) · (X_bar^INT8 · W_bar^INT8) · diag(Delta_W^FP16), applying per-token and per-channel scales only along the outer dimensions (T for activations, Co for weights) after the INT8 matrix multiplication completes, consistent with hardware-accelerated GEMM kernel constraints described in Section 3.

The core INT8 matrix multiplication X_bar^INT8 · W_bar^INT8 has been implemented such that both operands are INT8 tensors fed into an integer GEMM kernel, producing an INT32 (or equivalent higher-precision integer) accumulator output before any rescaling is applied, consistent with the inner term of Equation 2 in Section 3.

The per-token activation scale diag(Delta_X^FP16) is applied as a post-matmul multiplication along the outer token dimension T of the INT8 matmul's integer output, correctly broadcasting a single FP16 scale value per token/row rather than per input-channel, consistent with Equation 2 and the per-token/per-tensor granularity constraint described in Section 3.

The per-channel weight scale diag(Delta_W^FP16) is applied as a post-matmul multiplication along the outer output-channel dimension C_o of the INT8 matmul's integer output, correctly broadcasting a single FP16 scale value per output channel, consistent with Equation 2 and the per-channel/per-tensor granularity constraint described in Section 3.

The implementation enforces that scaling factors for the post-GEMM rescaling in Equation 2 can only be applied along the outer dimensions of the matrix multiplication (token dimension T for activations, output-channel dimension C_o for weights), and never along the inner (reduction/input-channel C_i) dimension, matching the hardware constraint explicitly described in Section 3: 'scaling can only be performed along the outer dimensions of the matrix multiplication ... which can be applied after the matrix multiplication finishes.'

The final output Y produced by combining diag(Delta_X^FP16) · (X_bar^INT8 · W_bar^INT8) · diag(Delta_W^FP16) is recovered as an FP16 tensor, matching the dequantized linear-layer output used downstream by subsequent FP16 elementwise operations (e.g., LayerNorm, activation functions) in the transformer block, consistent with Equation 2 in Section 3.

The implementation applies the activation-scale and weight-scale diagonal multiplications strictly after the INT8 matrix multiplication has fully completed (i.e., as a post-processing/epilogue step on the integer GEMM output), rather than interleaving any scaling operation within the matmul's inner accumulation loop, consistent with the statement in Section 3 that such scaling 'can be applied after the matrix multiplication finishes.'

The four baseline quantization schemes from Table 2 have been implemented: W8A8 naive (per-tensor weight, per-tensor dynamic activation), ZeroQuant (group-wise weight, per-token dynamic activation), LLM.int8() (per-channel weight, per-token dynamic activation + FP16 outlier decomposition), and Outlier Suppression (per-tensor weight, per-tensor static activation).

The W8A8 naive quantization baseline scheme has been implemented as specified in Table 2: per-tensor weight quantization combined with per-tensor dynamic activation quantization, with no smoothing transformation applied, serving as the simplest INT8 quantization baseline for comparison.

The W8A8 naive quantization baseline implements per-tensor weight quantization: a single quantization step size Delta is computed from the maximum absolute value across the entire weight matrix W and applied uniformly to quantize all weight elements to INT8, as specified for the 'W8A8' row of Table 2 (Weight column: 'per-tensor').

The W8A8 naive quantization baseline implements per-tensor dynamic activation quantization: a single quantization step size Delta is computed at runtime from the maximum absolute value across the entire activation tensor X for each forward pass (no offline calibration), and applied uniformly to quantize all activation elements to INT8, as specified for the 'W8A8' row of Table 2 (Activation column: 'per-tensor dynamic').

The W8A8 naive quantization baseline is implemented WITHOUT any SmoothQuant smoothing transformation applied: no per-channel smoothing factor s_j = max(|X_j|)^alpha / max(|W_j|)^(1-alpha) (Equation 4) is computed or applied to divide activations / multiply weights prior to quantization, ensuring this baseline represents the naive, unmodified quantization of the original FP16 activations and weights, distinguishing it from SmoothQuant-O1/O2/O3 which share the same per-tensor/per-tensor-dynamic granularity settings but DO apply the smoothing transformation beforehand.

It has been verified and documented that the W8A8 naive quantization scheme serves as the simplest INT8 quantization baseline in the paper's experiments, representing the case of applying standard per-tensor weight and per-tensor dynamic activation quantization directly to an LLM with no outlier-mitigation technique (no smoothing, no mixed precision, no group-wise or per-channel granularity), against which ZeroQuant, LLM.int8(), Outlier Suppression, and SmoothQuant-O1/O2/O3 are all compared in Tables 3, 4, and 5.

The ZeroQuant baseline quantization scheme has been implemented as specified in Table 2: group-wise weight quantization combined with per-token dynamic activation quantization, reproducing Yao et al. (2022)'s ZeroQuant method as described in Section 1 and Section 5.1.

The group-wise weight quantization mechanism used by the ZeroQuant baseline has been implemented, applying different quantization step sizes to different groups of channels within the weight matrix (a coarser-grained version of per-channel quantization), as specified for ZeroQuant in Table 2 (Weight column: 'group-wise') and described in Section 2 citing Shen et al. (2020) and Yao et al. (2022).

The per-token dynamic activation quantization mechanism used by the ZeroQuant baseline has been implemented, computing the quantization step size Delta at runtime independently for each token/row of the activation matrix (no offline calibration), as specified for ZeroQuant in Table 2 (Activation column: 'per-token dynamic').

It has been verified that the combined group-wise weight quantization plus per-token dynamic activation quantization implementation reproduces Yao et al. (2022)'s ZeroQuant method as referenced in Section 1 ('ZeroQuant (Yao et al., 2022) applies dynamic per-token activation quantization and group-wise weight quantization') and Section 5.1, with no SmoothQuant smoothing transformation applied to this baseline.

The LLM.int8() baseline quantization scheme has been implemented as specified in Table 2: per-channel weight quantization combined with per-token dynamic activation quantization plus FP16 mixed-precision outlier decomposition, reproducing Dettmers et al. (2022)'s LLM.int8() method as described in Section 1 and Section 5.1.

The per-channel weight quantization sub-mechanism used by the LLM.int8() baseline has been implemented: a distinct INT8 quantization step size is computed and applied for each output channel of the weight matrix W, as specified for LLM.int8() in Table 2 (Weight column: 'per-channel'), reproducing the weight-quantization component of Dettmers et al. (2022)'s method.

The per-token dynamic activation quantization sub-mechanism used by the LLM.int8() baseline has been implemented: for the non-outlier portion of the activation matrix, a quantization step size is computed at runtime independently for each token/row (no offline calibration), as specified for LLM.int8() in Table 2 (Activation column: 'per-token dynamic+FP16'), reproducing the dynamic activation-quantization component of Dettmers et al. (2022)'s method.

The outlier feature/channel detection sub-mechanism used by the LLM.int8() baseline has been implemented: activation channels containing values whose magnitude exceeds a threshold (identifying systematic outlier features) are detected at runtime prior to quantization, as required by Dettmers et al. (2022)'s mixed-precision decomposition method referenced in Section 1 and Table 2.

The outlier feature/channel detection sub-mechanism detects activation channels whose magnitude exceeds a fixed threshold, identifying systematic outlier features at runtime prior to quantization, as required by Dettmers et al. (2022)'s mixed-precision decomposition method referenced in Section 1 and Table 2.

The FP16 outlier computation path of the LLM.int8() baseline has been implemented: once outlier activation channels are detected, the corresponding activation values and their associated weight columns are kept in FP16 precision and multiplied using an FP16 matrix multiplication, separate from the INT8 path, as specified in Table 2 (Activation column: 'per-token dynamic+FP16') and described in Section 1: 'it keeps outliers in FP16 and uses INT8 for the other activations.'

The INT8 non-outlier computation path of the LLM.int8() baseline has been implemented: the non-outlier activation channels (quantized per-token dynamically) are multiplied against the correspondingly per-channel-quantized INT8 weight columns using an INT8 GEMM, separate from the FP16 outlier path, as specified in Table 2 and described in Section 1.

The combination step of the LLM.int8() mixed-precision decomposition has been implemented: the FP16 outlier-path partial result and the INT8 non-outlier-path partial result (dequantized back to FP16) are summed together to reconstruct the final linear-layer output Y, as required by the mixed-precision decomposition method of Dettmers et al. (2022) described in Section 1 and Table 2.

It has been verified that the LLM.int8() baseline implementation does NOT apply the SmoothQuant migration-strength smoothing transformation (i.e., the per-channel smoothing factor s_j = max(|X_j|)^alpha / max(|W_j|)^(1-alpha) from Equation 4 in Section 4, used to divide activations and multiply weight channels per Equation 3) prior to its per-channel weight quantization, per-token dynamic activation quantization, and FP16 mixed-precision outlier decomposition, confirming LLM.int8() is reproduced as an independent baseline method (Dettmers et al., 2022) distinct from SmoothQuant's own smoothing-based approach, as implied by Table 2 listing LLM.int8() separately from the SmoothQuant-O1/O2/O3 rows.

The FP16 mixed-precision decomposition mechanism used by the LLM.int8() baseline has been implemented: activation outlier features/channels are identified and kept in FP16 precision while the remaining (non-outlier) activation values are quantized to INT8, with the two precision paths combined to produce the final linear-layer output, as specified for LLM.int8() in Table 2 and described in Section 1 ('LLM.int8() addresses that accuracy issue by further introducing a mixed-precision decomposition (i.e., it keeps outliers in FP16 and uses INT8 for the other activations)').

The outlier feature/channel detection mechanism used by the LLM.int8() baseline has been implemented: activation channels containing values whose magnitude exceeds a fixed threshold are detected at runtime for each linear layer's input activations, prior to any quantization or precision splitting, as required for reproducing Dettmers et al. (2022)'s mixed-precision decomposition referenced in Section 1 and specified in Table 2's 'per-token dynamic+FP16' activation column for LLM.int8().

The Outlier Suppression baseline quantization scheme has been implemented as specified in Table 2: per-tensor weight quantization combined with per-tensor static activation quantization, reproducing Wei et al. (2022)'s Outlier Suppression method (non-scaling LayerNorm and token-wise clipping) as described in Section 6 (Related Work) and Section 5.1.

The three SmoothQuant quantization settings from Table 2 have been implemented: SmoothQuant-O1 (per-tensor static weight, per-token dynamic activation), SmoothQuant-O2 (per-tensor weight, per-tensor dynamic activation), and SmoothQuant-O3 (per-tensor weight, per-tensor static activation), each applied on top of the SmoothQuant smoothing transformation.

SmoothQuant-O1 has been implemented as specified in Table 2: per-tensor static weight quantization combined with per-token dynamic activation quantization, applied on top of the SmoothQuant smoothing transformation (Equation 3) using the per-channel smoothing factor s_j = max(|X_j|)^alpha / max(|W_j|)^(1-alpha) (Equation 4), representing the highest-accuracy but least-efficient of the three SmoothQuant settings.

SmoothQuant-O1 is defined and implemented exactly as specified in Table 2: the weight quantization column specifies 'per-tensor' (static, i.e. calibrated offline) and the activation quantization column specifies 'per-token dynamic', representing the highest-accuracy but least computationally efficient of the three SmoothQuant settings (O1, O2, O3), as described in Section 5.1 ('Baselines') and Table 2.

Prior to quantization in the SmoothQuant-O1 configuration, the activation smoothing procedure computes the per-channel smoothing factor s_j = max(|X_j|)^alpha / max(|W_j|)^(1-alpha) exactly as given in Equation 4 of Section 4, using the migration strength hyper-parameter alpha (with alpha=0.5 as the general sweet spot for OPT and BLOOM models, and alpha=0.75 for GLM-130B, per Section 5.1's 'Activation smoothing' paragraph) to control how much quantization difficulty is migrated from activations to weights.

In the SmoothQuant-O1 configuration, weight quantization is performed with per-tensor granularity using a statically calibrated quantization step size (computed offline from calibration data, per Table 2's 'per-tensor' weight setting), applied to the already-smoothed weight tensor diag(s)*W.

In the SmoothQuant-O1 configuration, activation quantization is performed with per-token granularity using dynamically computed quantization step sizes at runtime (a different step size is computed for each token/row of the activation matrix on every forward pass, per Table 2's 'per-token dynamic' activation setting), applied to the already-smoothed activation tensor X*diag(s)^-1.

It has been documented and verified that SmoothQuant-O1 is positioned as the highest-accuracy but least computationally efficient of the three SmoothQuant settings, consistent with Section 5.1's statement that 'the efficiency improves from O1 to O3 (i.e., lower latency)', and cross-verified against Table 11's latency ablation showing SmoothQuant-O1 consistently has the highest latency among the three SmoothQuant settings (e.g., OPT-13B seqlen 256: O1=124.5ms vs O2=120.5ms vs O3=112.1ms).

In the SmoothQuant-O1 configuration, the per-channel smoothing factor s_j (computed via s_j = max(|X_j|)^alpha / max(|W_j|)^(1-alpha), Equation 4) is applied to divide the input activations and multiply the corresponding weight channels (Equation 3) prior to per-tensor static weight quantization and per-token dynamic activation quantization, ensuring the smoothing transformation is correctly composed with the O1 quantization scheme.

SmoothQuant-O2 has been implemented as specified in Table 2: per-tensor weight quantization combined with per-tensor dynamic activation quantization, applied on top of the SmoothQuant smoothing transformation (Equation 3) using the per-channel smoothing factor s_j = max(|X_j|)^alpha / max(|W_j|)^(1-alpha) (Equation 4), representing an intermediate efficiency level between O1 and O3.

In the SmoothQuant-O2 configuration, weight quantization is performed with per-tensor granularity, using a single quantization step size Delta computed from the maximum absolute value across the entire (already-smoothed) weight tensor diag(s)*W, as specified in Table 2's 'SmoothQuant-O2' row (Weight column: 'per-tensor').

In the SmoothQuant-O2 configuration, activation quantization is performed with per-tensor dynamic granularity: a single quantization step size Delta is computed at runtime from the maximum absolute value across the entire (already-smoothed) activation tensor X*diag(s)^-1 on every forward pass (no offline calibration), as specified in Table 2's 'SmoothQuant-O2' row (Activation column: 'per-tensor dynamic').

Prior to quantization in the SmoothQuant-O2 configuration, the activation smoothing procedure computes the per-channel smoothing factor s_j = max(|X_j|)^alpha / max(|W_j|)^(1-alpha) exactly as given in Equation 4 of Section 4, using the migration strength hyper-parameter alpha (with alpha=0.5 as the general sweet spot for OPT and BLOOM models, and alpha=0.75 for GLM-130B, per Section 5.1's 'Activation smoothing' paragraph) to control how much quantization difficulty is migrated from activations to weights, and this computed smoothing factor is applied via Equation 3 (dividing activations by diag(s) and multiplying weights by diag(s)) before the per-tensor weight quantization and per-tensor dynamic activation quantization steps of SmoothQuant-O2 are performed.

It has been documented and verified that SmoothQuant-O2 is positioned as an intermediate efficiency level between O1 and O3, consistent with Section 5.1's statement that 'the efficiency improves from O1 to O3 (i.e., lower latency)', and cross-verified against Table 11's latency ablation showing SmoothQuant-O2's latency values fall strictly between SmoothQuant-O1 and SmoothQuant-O3 in every measured (model, sequence-length) configuration (e.g., OPT-13B seqlen 256: O1=124.5ms, O2=120.5ms, O3=112.1ms; OPT-13B seqlen 512: O1=243.3ms, O2=235.1ms, O3=223.1ms; OPT-30B seqlen 256: O1=246.7ms, O2=240.2ms, O3=227.6ms; OPT-30B seqlen 512: O1=490.7ms, O2=478.3ms, O3=458.4ms).

In the SmoothQuant-O2 configuration, the per-channel smoothing factor s_j (computed via s_j = max(|X_j|)^alpha / max(|W_j|)^(1-alpha), Equation 4) is applied to divide the input activations and multiply the corresponding weight channels (Equation 3) prior to per-tensor weight quantization and per-tensor dynamic activation quantization, ensuring the smoothing transformation is correctly composed with the O2 quantization scheme.

SmoothQuant-O3 has been implemented as specified in Table 2: per-tensor weight quantization combined with per-tensor static activation quantization, applied on top of the SmoothQuant smoothing transformation (Equation 3) using the per-channel smoothing factor s_j = max(|X_j|)^alpha / max(|W_j|)^(1-alpha) (Equation 4), representing the most aggressive and most efficient (lowest-latency) of the three SmoothQuant settings.

SmoothQuant-O3 is defined and implemented exactly as specified in Table 2: the weight quantization column specifies 'per-tensor' and the activation quantization column specifies 'per-tensor static', representing the most aggressive and most computationally efficient (lowest-latency) of the three SmoothQuant settings (O1, O2, O3), as described in Section 5.1 ('Baselines') and Table 2.

Prior to quantization in the SmoothQuant-O3 configuration, the activation smoothing procedure computes the per-channel smoothing factor s_j = max(|X_j|)^alpha / max(|W_j|)^(1-alpha) exactly as given in Equation 4 of Section 4, using the migration strength hyper-parameter alpha (with alpha=0.5 as the general sweet spot for OPT and BLOOM models, and alpha=0.75 for GLM-130B, per Section 5.1's 'Activation smoothing' paragraph) to control how much quantization difficulty is migrated from activations to weights, and this computed smoothing factor s is then applied via Equation 3 (dividing activations by diag(s) and multiplying weights by diag(s)) before the per-tensor weight quantization and per-tensor static activation quantization steps of SmoothQuant-O3 are performed.

In the SmoothQuant-O3 configuration, weight quantization is performed with per-tensor granularity, using a single quantization step size Delta computed from the maximum absolute value across the entire (already-smoothed) weight tensor diag(s)*W, as specified in Table 2's 'SmoothQuant-O3' row (Weight column: 'per-tensor').

In the SmoothQuant-O3 configuration, activation quantization is performed with per-tensor static granularity: a single quantization step size Delta is calibrated offline (using the 512-sentence Pile calibration set, per Section 5.1) from the maximum absolute value across the entire (already-smoothed) activation tensor X*diag(s)^-1, and this fixed step size is reused at inference time (no runtime recomputation), as specified in Table 2's 'SmoothQuant-O3' row (Activation column: 'per-tensor static').

It has been documented and verified that SmoothQuant-O3 is positioned as the most aggressive and most computationally efficient (lowest-latency) of the three SmoothQuant settings, consistent with Section 5.1's statement that 'the efficiency improves from O1 to O3 (i.e., lower latency)', and cross-verified against Table 11's latency ablation showing SmoothQuant-O3 consistently has the lowest latency among the three SmoothQuant settings across all measured configurations (e.g., OPT-13B seqlen 256: O1=124.5ms, O2=120.5ms, O3=112.1ms; OPT-13B seqlen 512: O1=243.3ms, O2=235.1ms, O3=223.1ms; OPT-30B seqlen 256: O1=246.7ms, O2=240.2ms, O3=227.6ms; OPT-30B seqlen 512: O1=490.7ms, O2=478.3ms, O3=458.4ms).

In the SmoothQuant-O3 configuration, the per-channel smoothing factor s_j (computed via s_j = max(|X_j|)^alpha / max(|W_j|)^(1-alpha), Equation 4) is applied to divide the input activations and multiply the corresponding weight channels (Equation 3) prior to per-tensor weight quantization and per-tensor static activation quantization, ensuring the smoothing transformation is correctly composed with the O3 quantization scheme.

It has been verified that the same activation-smoothing computation (Equation 4's migration strength alpha formula) and the same mathematically equivalent scale-migration transformation (Equation 3) are applied identically across all three SmoothQuant settings (O1, O2, O3), with the only differences between the three settings being the downstream weight/activation quantization granularity and static-vs-dynamic mode as defined in Table 2, confirming SmoothQuant's smoothing mechanism is orthogonal to and reusable across all quantization efficiency levels, as stated in Section 1: 'Since SmoothQuant is compatible with various quantization schemes, we implement three efficiency levels of quantization settings for SmoothQuant.'

The same activation-smoothing computation (Equation 4's migration strength alpha formula) and the same scale-migration transformation (Equation 3) are applied identically across all three SmoothQuant settings (O1, O2, O3), as stated in Section 1: 'Since SmoothQuant is compatible with various quantization schemes, we implement three efficiency levels of quantization settings for SmoothQuant.'

The only differences between the O1, O2, and O3 SmoothQuant settings are the downstream weight/activation quantization granularity and static-vs-dynamic mode as defined in Table 2, confirming the smoothing mechanism is orthogonal to and reusable across all quantization efficiency levels.

The implementation exposes a configurable mechanism (e.g., a setting/flag) to select among SmoothQuant-O1, SmoothQuant-O2, and SmoothQuant-O3 for a given model run, correctly mapping each selection to its corresponding weight/activation quantization granularity and static/dynamic mode combination as defined in Table 2, while always applying the shared SmoothQuant smoothing transformation beforehand.

The codebase implements a configurable mechanism (e.g., a command-line flag, config parameter, or enum setting) that allows the user to select one of SmoothQuant-O1, SmoothQuant-O2, or SmoothQuant-O3 for a given model quantization run, as implied by Section 5.1's statement that 'we implement three efficiency levels of quantization settings for SmoothQuant.'

Selecting O1 in the configurable mechanism correctly instantiates per-tensor static weight quantization plus per-token dynamic activation quantization; selecting O2 correctly instantiates per-tensor weight quantization plus per-tensor dynamic activation quantization; and selecting O3 correctly instantiates per-tensor weight quantization plus per-tensor static activation quantization, exactly matching the three SmoothQuant rows of Table 2.

Regardless of which O1/O2/O3 configuration is selected, the implementation first computes the per-channel smoothing factor s_j = max(|X_j|)^alpha / max(|W_j|)^(1-alpha) (Equation 4 in Section 4) using the migration strength hyper-parameter alpha, and applies this smoothing transformation (dividing activations by diag(s) and multiplying weights by diag(s), per Equation 3) prior to branching into the O1/O2/O3-specific weight/activation quantization granularity and static/dynamic mode logic, as stated in Section 4: 'Here we introduce a hyper-parameter, migration strength α, to control how much difficulty we want to migrate from activation to weights, using the following equation: s_j = max(|X_j|)^α / max(|W_j|)^(1−α).'

The full quantization flow for transformer blocks (Figure 6) has been implemented, quantizing all compute-heavy operators (linear layers and BMM attention operators) to INT8 while keeping lightweight element-wise operators in FP16, as described in Section 4 ('Applying SmoothQuant to Transformer blocks').
